sources_considered.why: Detailed legal research describes China's operative national rules and their scope.
Primary summary by the AI Index team reports historical model-performance convergence.
Readable mirror of a Congressional Research Service report compares the national regulatory approaches and records the US legislative position.
The PDF exceeded the reader's size limit; the team's readable summary was used instead.

evidence_items.publisher: Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance
evidence_items.locator: Abstract; section Overview of China’s approach to regulating AI
evidence_items.explanation: The article describes the existing national generative-AI measures alongside algorithm-recommendation and deep-synthesis rules. These impose provider obligations, although the generative-AI measures exclude research and applications not serving the public.

evidence_items.publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence

receipt.public_excerpt: China is closing the performance gap.

evidence_items.explanation: The section reports that gaps on MMLU and HumanEval fell from double digits in 2023 to near parity in 2024. It also records continued US leadership in the number of notable models, so convergence does not mean leadership on every measure.

evidence_items.publisher: Congressional Research Service, hosted by EveryCRSReport
evidence_items.locator: Federal Laws Addressing AI, concluding paragraph
evidence_items.explanation: The report reviews federal enactments as of May 2025 and describes China's national provider rules. Together with e1, it supports a qualitative difference in AI-specific regulatory coverage, rather than a precise ratio of laws.

unresolved_gaps: These sources do not estimate whether China's regulation slowed progress relative to an unregulated counterfactual.
The relative amount of regulation is qualitative, not a harmonized numerical count.
